teaching.hint: Which end of a root-to-leaf path becomes the first and most significant character of its candidate string?

solution_outline.decisive_insight: The first character of a candidate is at the leaf, so a locally smaller root-side branch need not produce the smallest complete string.
solution_outline.approach: Traverse every root-to-leaf path while retaining its letters. At each leaf, read that path in reverse to obtain one full candidate and keep the smallest candidate seen.
solution_outline.state_and_invariant: The traversal buffer contains exactly the root-to-current-node letters. The running best is the lexicographically smallest completed leaf-to-root string among leaves already visited.
solution_outline.correctness: Every leaf determines one and only one candidate path. Reversing its buffered path gives the required leaf-first order, and comparing that candidate with the running minimum preserves the minimum of all candidates seen. Visiting every leaf therefore returns the global minimum, including prefix-length tie behavior.
solution_outline.complexity: O(n + Lh) time for n nodes, L leaves, and tree height h because each leaf may reverse and compare a length-h path; O(h) auxiliary space for the traversal path, stack, and best candidate.
solution_outline.pitfall: Choosing the smaller-valued child near the root is unsound because that letter appears near the end, not the beginning, of the candidate string.

accepted_alternatives: Prepend each node's letter to a copied partial string during DFS, then compare complete strings at leaves; this uses O(nh) time and O(h^2) live path-copy space in a skewed tree.
common_wrong_turns: Append letters in root-to-leaf order and compare that string
Greedily choose a smaller child before seeing leaves
Treat node value zero as an absent-node marker
source_fidelity_notes: Image-only examples were replaced by a small textual tree; leaf-to-root reading, prefix tie rule, value mapping, and node count were retained.
